overview.title: 📖 Overview: Closing the Firstborn Donkey Dispute
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 10a–10b
overview.hebrewSource: וְעָרַפְתּוֹ... נֶאֱמַר כָּאן עֲרִיפָה וְנֶאֱמַר לְהַלָּן עֲרִיפָה
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf continues probing whether an item's prohibition alone can render it 'food' susceptible to impurity, using a crow slaughtered only for practice as a test case. It then works to prove, through several independent routes, that even Rabbi Shimon — who generally permits benefit from an unredeemed firstborn donkey — concedes that once its neck is broken, all benefit is forbidden. A close reading of one baraita distinguishes benefit from the donkey's value from benefit from its body, before the daf turns to a betrothal puzzle and closes with the mechanics of redemption: how soon, and for how little, a firstborn donkey may be redeemed.

slides.title: 🐦 Does a Forbidden Item Count as 'Food'?
slides.subtitle: A crow slaughtered only to practice slaughtering

lines.speaker: Nimos
lines.text: One who slaughters a crow just to practice — its blood still renders other foods susceptible to impurity, but the crow itself needs separate intent to count as food.

lines.speaker: R' Eliezer
lines.text: No — slaughter-blood always renders food susceptible, and even the crow itself needs no extra intent. Its very prohibition is its intent.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Does this prove the general rule 'its prohibition is its intent'? Maybe not — perhaps Rabbi Eliezer's leniency is special to a crow, which has some kosher-bird features.

lines.speaker: Rava
lines.text: Resolved: everyone agrees we do not say 'its prohibition is its intent.' The real issue is whether kosher-like features alone create food-status.

slides.title: ⚰️ Rava's Proof: Even Rabbi Shimon Forbids Benefit After the Neck Is Broken
slides.subtitle: An argument from a baraita's silence

nodes.content: ❓ Rabbi Shimon generally treats forbidden-benefit items as not susceptible to food-impurity — shouldn't a neck-broken donkey be exempt too?
📜 A baraita lists Rabbi Shimon's exceptions — orla, diverse kinds, a stoned ox, an eglah arufah, a metzora's birds, meat-in-milk — but a broken-necked donkey is not among them
✅ Silence is proof: if benefit were still permitted, the baraita would list the donkey too. Since it doesn't, Rabbi Shimon must hold benefit is forbidden at that stage
🔁 Rav Naḥman independently confirms this: 'breaking the neck' (עֲרִיפָה) here matches the same word used for the eglah arufah, whose carcass is forbidden

slides.title: 📜 One Baraita, Two Kinds of Benefit
slides.subtitle: Why the dispute is stated twice, for two different forms of benefit
rows: First clause: if not redeemed, its neck is broken and it's buried; 'forbidden benefit' (R' Yehuda) vs. permitted (R' Shimon)
Benefit from the donkey's monetary value — renting or selling it — while alive
Second clause: one may not kill it any other way; shearing and labor forbidden (R' Yehuda) vs. permitted (R' Shimon)
Benefit from the animal itself — shearing, labor — while alive

callout.label: Why state both?
callout.text: Each ruling alone might be mistaken as the case where the other sage concedes — stating both closes that gap and confirms the dispute spans both kinds of benefit.

slides.title: 🐴 A Betrothal Puzzle
slides.subtitle: Which opinion does 'she is not betrothed' follow?

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: A mishna rules: one who betroths a woman with a firstborn donkey — she is not betrothed, since benefit from it is forbidden. Does the mishna reject Rabbi Shimon entirely?

lines.speaker: Rav Naḥman
lines.text: No — it's speaking about after the neck is broken, where even Rabbi Shimon agrees benefit is forbidden.

lines.speaker: Alt. view
lines.text: But maybe it follows neither sage as stated: if Rabbi Shimon, she should be betrothed with the full value; if Rabbi Yehuda, with the difference between the donkey's and the lamb's value.

lines.speaker: Rabba bar Avuh
lines.text: Resolved: it follows Rabbi Yehuda, in a case where the donkey is worth only a shekel — exactly the lamb's minimum value, leaving no difference to betroth with at all.

slides.title: 💰 Redeeming Immediately, For Any Amount — Or Not Less Than a Shekel?
slides.subtitle: Two readings of the redemption verse

steps.content: 1️⃣ The doubled verb 'תפדה...תפדה' (you shall redeem) teaches two things: redeem the donkey immediately after birth, and redeem it for any amount, however small
2️⃣ Why not learn instead from a firstborn son — redeemed after 30 days, for a fixed 5 shekels? The doubled verb overrides that comparison entirely
3️⃣ Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda disagrees: no redemption is valid for less than a shekel's worth, from 'all your valuations shall be by the sacred shekel' (Leviticus 27:25)
4️⃣ This shekel-minimum applies even though Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda does not compare the donkey's redemption to the human firstborn's five-shekel price

summary.principle: A firstborn donkey's forbidden status while unredeemed is real but limited: Rabbi Shimon permits benefit from a live donkey, yet even he concedes that once its neck is broken all benefit ceases — and its redemption must happen immediately, for any amount no less than a shekel.

flowSteps.content: 🐦 A forbidden item's food-status turns on kosher-like features, not on 'its prohibition being its intent'
⚰️ Multiple proofs converge: even Rabbi Shimon forbids benefit from a firstborn donkey once its neck is broken

columns.content: 📜 The Yehuda/Shimon dispute spans both monetary value and direct use of a live donkey
🐴 A betrothal mishna is reconciled with both opinions through careful case-narrowing

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: redemption must happen immediately, for any amount — though Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda sets a shekel floor

quiz.q: According to Rava's conclusion, what actually explains why some forbidden items (like the meat of a camel or crow) are susceptible to food-impurity without special intent?
o: The principle that 'its prohibition serves as its intent'
Their possession of some kosher-animal characteristics, not the prohibition itself
A direct verse naming each animal
Rabbinic decree with no textual basis
quiz.e: Rava concludes that everyone agrees we do not say 'its prohibition serves as its intent'; instead, items with some kosher-like features are treated as food regardless of intent.

quiz.q: How does Rava prove that even Rabbi Shimon forbids benefit from a firstborn donkey after its neck has been broken?
o: A verse states it explicitly for Rabbi Shimon
A baraita lists Rabbi Shimon's exceptions to the 'forbidden items aren't food' rule, and a broken-necked donkey is conspicuously absent from that list
Rabbi Shimon later retracted his opinion
It is derived from the laws of a stoned ox
quiz.e: Since the baraita lists Rabbi Shimon's specific exceptions but omits a neck-broken donkey, its absence implies Rabbi Shimon holds it remains forbidden and therefore isn't 'food' at all.

quiz.q: Why does the baraita need to state the Yehuda/Shimon dispute both regarding the donkey's monetary value AND its use for labor/shearing?
o: Because the two statements are redundant and could be combined
Because each ruling alone might be mistaken as a case where the other sage concedes, so both must be stated
Because they refer to different animals entirely
Because only Rabbi Yehuda discusses monetary value
quiz.e: Without both clauses, one might assume Rabbi Shimon concedes on one type of benefit while disputing the other; stating both confirms the dispute covers both forms.

quiz.q: According to Rav Naḥman's proof, why does even Rabbi Shimon agree that benefit is forbidden after a firstborn donkey's neck is broken?
o: Because dead animals are always forbidden
Because a verbal analogy links 'breaking the neck' here to the same phrase used for the eglah arufah, whose carcass is likewise forbidden
Because the priest must consent to any use
Because Rabbi Shimon never permits killing the donkey at all
quiz.e: Rav Naḥman derives from the shared term 'breaking the neck' (arifah) that the prohibition on deriving benefit from the eglah arufah's carcass applies equally to a neck-broken firstborn donkey.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, what is the minimum value required to redeem a firstborn donkey, and from where is it derived?
o: Five shekels, by comparison to redeeming a firstborn son
Not less than a shekel, derived from 'all your valuations shall be by the sacred shekel' (Leviticus 27:25)
Any amount at all, with no minimum
Ten shekels, by rabbinic decree
quiz.e: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda derives a shekel minimum from the general valuation verse in Leviticus, not from any comparison to the five-shekel redemption of a firstborn son.
